newsitem.title: SOLOMON ISLANDS: Solomon Islands goes to polls by canoe and aircraf.
newsitem.headline: Solomon Islands goes to polls by canoe and aircraf.

text.p: The scattered South Pacific archipelago of the Solomon Islands went to the polls on Wednesday, but with islands stretching over 1,400 km (870 miles) of ocean, final votes will not be counted for a week.
Election officials said the bulk of the US$1.0 million election budget will go to hiring motorised canoes and aircraft to reach the far-flung, mountainous and jungle-covered islands.
Political analysts said prime minister Solomon Mamaloni faces little opposition and is favoured to secure a fourth term as prime minister.
"He stands a very good chance as a candidate," a spokesman for Mamaloni told Reuters on Wednesday.
"But we are not saying anything about the prime minister as it's so unpredictable when the parties get into parliament."

Mamaloni gained a third term as prime minister in November 1994 through a parliamentary vote, after losing a similar vote following the May 1993 election, in which his party gained the most seats but fell short of a majority.
Analysts said the charismatic, betel-nut chewing Mamaloni is likely to be forced into another shaky coalition government.
Mamaloni's National Unity party is expected to win up to 20 seats in a new 50-seat, one house parliament. Mamaloni's party only held 21 seats out of 47 in the old parliament.
With nine political parties and 350 candidates contesting the election, personality politics dominates, with economic management and political corruption the only issues.
The Solomon Islands, with a population of 400,000, has one of the weakest economies in the South Pacific, relying on cocoa, copra, fish and timber exports.
Unlike other island nations, income from tourism is minimal.
The Solomon Islands economy slowed down in calendar 1996, growing by three to four percent compared with seven percent in the previous year, the central bank said in its 1996 report.
"Unless government finance problems are resolved, similar problems are expected to occur in 1997," the bank said.

The former British protectorate achieved its greatest fame during the Second World War when it was the scene of some the fiercest land and naval battles between Japan and the Allies and names such as Guadalcanal, The Slot and Henderson Field became known the world over.
